records.our_prose: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, onions are a one-time spring crop. In the warmer Coastal Plain (zone 8) grow intermediate-day onions, set out early from late February into late March so they build size before the day-length trigger; true short-day (Southern) types are the traditional choice in the southern Coastal Plain. The cooler Piedmont (zone 7) is long-day onion country. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the ground can be worked; onions shrug off a light frost. They are ready mid-to-late summer when about half the tops flop over and dry. Pull them, then cure in a warm, airy spot for two to four weeks before storing.

records.our_prose: Onion in the Mid-Atlantic is a single spring-planted crop with no fall crop. Day-length suitability splits by zone: the cooler Piedmont north (zone 7) is long-day onion country, while the Coastal Plain south (zone 8, at or below the 36°N line) is intermediate-day country, where NC State recommends short-day types for eastern North Carolina and calls long-day onions not recommended there. Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a spring window and no fall column; for the intermediate-day Coastal Plain we close the planting window by the end of March, about Feb 20 to Mar 31 in zone 8, rather than running to the table's April date, since intermediate-day onions size up best when set early, while the long-day Piedmont keeps the fuller spring window, about Mar 1 to May 1 in zone 7. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the soil is workable, well ahead of the last frost since onion is cold-hardy. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage.

records.our_prose: Onion in the Mid-South is a single spring-planted crop with no fall crop. This belt is intermediate-day onion country: it sits around and below the 36°N line where growers move off long-day types, so intermediate-day varieties (the widely adaptable Candy is the regional standard) are the reliable pick, with short-day (Southern) types also succeeding in the lowland south and long-day types workable only at the cooler northern edge. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the soil is workable, roughly mid February into late March in zone 8 and about a week and a half later in the cooler zone 7 uplands; intermediate-day onions size up best when set early, so the window closes by the end of March rather than running into April. Onion is cold-hardy and goes in well before the last frost. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage. University of Arkansas, Oklahoma State, and University of Tennessee Extension all steer this belt to short-day or intermediate-day onions.

records.our_prose: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 to 7), onion is a single spring-planted crop. Grow long-day cultivars: they need 14 to 16 hours of daylight to bulb, which northern summers deliver, and they build a full leaf canopy before the solstice trigger so bulbs size up large. Start seed indoors about 10 weeks ahead (sow in February for a May transplant in the coldest zones), then set cold-hardy transplants or sets out as soon as the soil is workable, roughly two weeks before the last frost. Bulbs mature in mid-to-late summer when about half the tops fall over; lift and cure them two to four weeks before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant: planting stays anchored to frost and workable soil. The bolting trap here is cold-driven, not day-length driven, so it stays minor for a spring crop set as a small transplant, but oversized sets exposed to a cold snap can run to seed instead of bulbing.

records.our_prose: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9), onion is a fall-planted, overwintering short-day crop. Grow short-day cultivars: they bulb at only 10 to 12 hours of daylight, which the region's mild fall and winter provide. Start seed in early-to-mid fall, then set transplants or sets from November through February so the plant builds a strong leaf canopy over winter before short days trigger bulbing. Bulbs mature in mid-spring, harvested April into May before summer heat; lift when about half the tops fall and cure before storage. Day length gates which cultivar bulbs here, not when you plant. The central pitfall is bolting: a transplant or set that is too large going into winter cold vernalizes and runs to seed instead of bulbing, so use pencil-sized or smaller transplants and sets under half an inch.

These are grown in southern states generally below the 35th parallel, and are not suitable for bulb production in the northwest, except as pearl or boiler varieties, or for overwinter production.
